title: Given an integer array and an integer K, count the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly K. The array may contain negative numbers.
shortTitle: Subarray Sum Equals K — Prefix Sum Plus a HashMap Counting currentSum Minus K

s1_definition.profdef: Counting subarrays that sum to K uses a running prefix sum combined with a HashMap that records how many times each prefix sum value has occurred. At each index we look up how many earlier prefixes equal currentSum minus K, because each such earlier prefix marks the start of a subarray summing to K. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space and handles negative numbers, which a sliding window cannot.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank tracks a running net cash position day by day. To count how many date ranges had a net change of exactly K rupees, the clerk keeps a tally of how often each running total has appeared so far. On each day, if the running total minus K has appeared before, each earlier occurrence pins down a date range that nets exactly K.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a running sum and a count of seen sums; at each step add how many times currentSum minus K was seen.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting subarrays that sum to K uses a running prefix sum combined with a HashMap that records how many times each prefix sum value has occurred. At each index we look up how many earlier prefixes equal currentSum minus K, because each such earlier prefix marks the start of a subarray summing to K. This runs in O(n) time and O(n) space and handles negative numbers, which a sliding window cannot.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank tracks a running net cash position day by day. To count how many date ranges had a net change of exactly K rupees, the clerk keeps a tally of how often each running total has appeared so far. On each day, if the running total minus K has appeared before, each earlier occurrence pins down a date range that nets exactly K.

**One line to remember:** Keep a running sum and a count of seen sums; at each step add how many times currentSum minus K was seen.

sections.s2_technical:
The core identity is that a subarray from index i plus one to j sums to K exactly when prefix[j] minus prefix[i] equals K, which rearranges to prefix[i] equals prefix[j] minus K. So at each position j, the number of valid subarrays ending at j equals the number of earlier prefix values equal to currentSum minus K.

We do this in one pass without a full prefix array, using a HashMap from prefix-sum value to its occurrence count. We seed the map with `map.put(0, 1)` so that a prefix that itself equals K, meaning a subarray from the very start, is counted. For example, if currentSum becomes K at some index, currentSum minus K is 0, and the seeded zero contributes one count.

The loop is `int count = 0, sum = 0; for (int x : nums) { sum += x; count += map.getOrDefault(sum - K, 0); map.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum); }`. The order matters: we add to the count before recording the current sum, so we never count a zero-length subarray.

Because this method relies on prefix-sum differences rather than monotonic window growth, it correctly handles negative numbers, which is the key reason a sliding window does not work here; a window assumes adding elements only increases the sum, which fails when values can be negative.

A senior-level nuance is the map-seeding of zero, which is the most common bug if forgotten, because it is what lets subarrays that begin at index zero be counted. Another nuance is that the map stores counts, not just presence, because a given prefix sum can recur multiple times and each recurrence is a distinct valid starting point.

The time is O(n) with one pass and O(n) worst-case space for the map, which is a big improvement over the O(n squared) brute force of checking every subarray.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India monitors a stream of signed daily net cash movements for an account, where deposits are positive and withdrawals are negative. Compliance wants to count how many contiguous date ranges had a net movement of exactly a flagged amount K, as a pattern-detection signal. Because movements can be negative, a sliding window will not work. This is exactly the subarray-sum-equals-K problem.

Problem 2 — The brute-force check of every possible date range is quadratic and too slow on long histories, so we use the prefix-sum-plus-HashMap method for a single linear pass.

Problem 3 — The map must be seeded with a zero prefix having count one, so that ranges starting from the first day are counted correctly.

In the code: a `SubarrayCounter` has a `countSubarrays` method implementing the running-sum HashMap technique. A `SubarrayDemo` main counts ranges summing to K in a signed movement array.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: movements 1, 2, 3, minus 2, 5 and K equals 5. The ranges summing to 5 are 2 plus 3, the single 5 at the end, and 3 minus 2 plus 5 minus 1... let me trace precisely.

Step 0: seen is zero mapped to one. sum 0, count 0.

Step 1 (x 1): sum 1. We look up sum minus K, 1 minus 5 equals minus 4, not seen, add 0. Record sum 1 with count 1. count 0.

Step 2 (x 2): sum 3. Look up 3 minus 5 equals minus 2, not seen, add 0. Record sum 3. count 0.

Step 3 (x 3): sum 6. Look up 6 minus 5 equals 1, seen once, add 1. This is the range 2 plus 3 equals 5. Record sum 6. count 1.

Step 4 (x minus 2): sum 4. Look up 4 minus 5 equals minus 1, not seen, add 0. Record sum 4. count 1.

Step 5 (x 5): sum 9. Look up 9 minus 5 equals 4, seen once, add 1. This is the range from after the prefix-4 point to the end, which is 5. count 2. Record sum 9.

Final count is 2: the range 2,3 and the range 5.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 23:10:00 [INFO] Counting date ranges with net movement exactly K=5
2026-10-26 23:10:00 [INFO] Number of matching ranges -> 2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting the contiguous subarrays that sum to exactly K is a prefix-sum problem combined with a HashMap of previously seen prefix sums. The core identity is that a subarray sums to K precisely when the running prefix sum at its end minus the running prefix sum just before its start equals K, which rearranges to say an earlier prefix must equal the current running sum minus K. So I keep a running sum and a map that counts how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred, and at each element I add to my answer the number of earlier prefixes equal to the current sum minus K, because each one marks the start of a valid subarray ending here.

Two details are essential. First, I seed the map with a prefix sum of zero having a count of one, which is what lets subarrays that begin at the very first element be counted, and forgetting this seed is the single most common bug. Second, I add to the answer before recording the current prefix sum, so I never count a zero-length range. The whole thing is a single linear pass using linear space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, compliance monitors a stream of signed daily net cash movements, deposits positive and withdrawals negative, and wants to count how many contiguous date ranges netted exactly a flagged amount as a pattern-detection signal. Crucially the movements can be negative, which is why I use this prefix-sum-and-map method rather than a sliding window. A sliding window assumes that extending the window only increases the sum, and that assumption breaks the moment negative values appear, so it would give wrong counts.

This also replaces the naive quadratic approach of checking every possible range with a single linear scan, which is the difference between a query that runs instantly and one that times out on a long transaction history. Being able to explain why the window technique fails here, and why the prefix-sum-map technique does not, is exactly the kind of reasoning that distinguishes a strong candidate.
